newsitem.title: USA: Slump in October homebuilding confirms waning momentum. [CORRECTED 01:05 GMT 20/11]
newsitem.headline: Slump in October homebuilding confirms waning momentum. [CORRECTED 01:05 GMT 20/11]

text.p: Construction starts on new homes and apartments slumped sharply in October to the slowest rate in a year, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, as the key housing sector steadily lost momentum.

Total starts dropped 5.1 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.366 million after a steep 6.1 percent fall in September (Corrects from "October"). It was the weakest building rate since 1.351 million a year in October 1995.
Analysts said the sizzle was going out of the building industry after a hearty first half in which builders were hard pressed to keep up with demand.
New applications for building permits declined for a third month in a row last month, hinting at a further waning in the pace of construction in coming months.

"During the third quarter we started to lose steam for sure and now we're moving into the fourth quarter on a weaker note yet," said David Seiders, an economist at the National Association of Home Builders.
"The hope now is that the recent fall in long-term (interest) rates will help to stabilize things," he added.

Mortgage rates were lower in October than they were a month earlier, averaging 7.85 percent for a 30-year loan compared with 8.23 percent in September. Last week, average rates for a long-term mortgage were down to 7.59 percent.

The report of weaker October homebuilding sparked a rally on bond markets, where prices on 30-year bonds were up $4.688 on a $1,000 bond at midday. The yield, which moves in the opposite direction to prices, was down to 6.43 percent from 6.46 percent at Monday's close.

The housing industry has an overarching impact on the overall economy because it is a major employer and buying or buidling commitments spawn a range of spending, from purchases of building materials to furniture.
The falloff in construction during October was widespread.

Building rates for single-family homes fell 4.6 percent to 1.069 million a year, the weakest performance since 1.036 million in June 1995. Starts on apartments dropped 7.2 percent to a rate of 297,000.
Overall growth in the national economy, measured by gross domestic product, throttled back to an annual 2.2 percent rate in the third quarter from a booming 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
Weak October homebuilding will contribute to continued slow GDP growth for the rest of the year.
"The decline indicates that housing starts will be a drag on the economy in the fourth quarter," said economist Elliott Platt of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.

On Monday, the National Association of Home Builders said its index of market activity again dropped 4 points in November to 51 from 55 in October as sales and visitor traffic to model sites eased off.
"The very strong level of housing activity achieved in the first half of the year simply could not be sustained," said association President Randy Smith, a builder in Walnut Creek, Calif.
Regionally, housing starts fell everywhere last month except in the West, where they increased 6.5 percent to an annual rate of 358,000.
In the Northeast, they declined 9.3 percent to 127,000 a year and in the Midwest they were down 9.2 percent to a rate of 277,000. Housing starts in the South fell 8.3 percent to 604,000 a year.
